notes: Class B document (14 units). Covers ionic vs covalent bonding with electron transfer/sharing diagrams. One ECU for worked example.

units.label: Title: Chemical Bonding: Ionic and Covalent
Hook: table salt vs water (image)
units.content_summary: Side-by-side photo of table salt crystals (NaCl) and water droplets. Caption: 'Both are made of bonded atoms — but the bonds work very differently.'

units.label: Learning Objectives (text)
units.content_summary: Objectives: explain why atoms bond; distinguish ionic from covalent bonds; predict bond type from electronegativity difference; draw simple Lewis structures.

units.label: Why atoms bond: octet rule (text)
units.content_summary: Atoms bond to achieve a stable electron configuration, typically 8 valence electrons (octet rule). Bonding lowers the overall energy of the system, making the bonded state more stable than separate atoms.

units.label: Ionic bonding: electron transfer (text)
units.content_summary: Ionic bonds form when one atom transfers electrons to another, typically between a metal and nonmetal. Example: Na gives its 1 valence electron to Cl, forming Na+ and Cl-, which attract electrostatically.

units.label: Ionic bonding diagram (image)
units.content_summary: Diagram showing Na atom transferring one electron to Cl atom, forming Na+ and Cl- ions held together by electrostatic attraction, forming NaCl crystal lattice.

units.label: Covalent bonding: electron sharing (text)
units.content_summary: Covalent bonds form when atoms share electron pairs, typically between two nonmetals. Example: two H atoms share one electron pair each to form H2, both achieving a stable duet configuration.

units.label: Covalent bonding diagram (image)
units.content_summary: Diagram showing two hydrogen atoms overlapping electron clouds to share a pair of electrons, forming H2 molecule with a single covalent bond.

units.label: Electronegativity and bond prediction (text)
units.content_summary: Electronegativity difference predicts bond type: large difference (>1.7) → ionic; small difference (<1.7, >0.4) → polar covalent; near zero → nonpolar covalent. A simple rule of thumb for classifying compounds.

units.label: Worked example: classify NaCl and H2O (text)
units.content_summary: NaCl: electronegativity difference ≈2.1 (Na=0.9, Cl=3.0) → ionic. H2O: difference ≈1.4 (H=2.1, O=3.5) → polar covalent. Both classifications explained with the electronegativity table.

units.label: Electronegativity table (image)
units.content_summary: Small periodic table excerpt showing electronegativity values for common elements (H, C, N, O, Na, Cl) used in the worked example.

units.label: Video: bonding types comparison (video)
units.content_summary: Animated video contrasting ionic bond formation (electron transfer, crystal lattice) with covalent bond formation (electron sharing, discrete molecules) side by side.

units.label: Practice: classify five compounds (text)
units.content_summary: Five compounds given (MgO, CO2, KBr, CH4, CaCl2); classify each as ionic or covalent using electronegativity differences.
